transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. Honestly, I'm just at my wit's end here. What brings me in is that I... I just can't seem to keep my mind on a task long enough to actually finish it anymore. And it's not just the mundane stuff, it happens even when it's incredibly important. 

I'm a computer support specialist, and I have a graduate degree, so I've been doing complex technical work for a long time. I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing. But lately, I'll sit down to do something like, say, tracing a client's network problem—which is a very standard procedure for me, usually a high priority—and I'll pull up the server logs to look for the error. And then, I don't know, ten or maybe fifteen minutes will go by, and I'll suddenly realize that I've just been staring at the exact same lines on the screen. I'll have reread the same three log entries over and over and over again, and I still have absolutely no idea what they even say. 

It's like the words just aren't registering, or my brain just completely unplugs from what's right in front of me. It's incredibly frustrating because I know how to do my job, the clients are waiting on me to fix their systems, but I just can't force my brain to stay locked in on the screen long enough to get through the data. I just sit there and realize I've lost a huge chunk of time accomplishing absolutely nothing, and it's really starting to become a severe problem for me at work.
Have you also been feeling unusually restless, fidgety, or have trouble staying seated, especially when trying to focus on tasks?

Oh, God, yes. Yes to all of that. It's... it's constant, really. I mean, you would think at fifty-three years old I'd have learned how to just sit quietly in a chair, but it's like I have this physical motor humming inside me that just won't shut off, especially when I'm forced to sit there and try to focus on something. 

Like, for instance, when I'm sitting right there at a desk with a client—which happens a lot in my line of work, you know, they're hovering over my shoulder while I'm trying to explain what went wrong with their hardware—my leg will just be bouncing a mile a minute under the desk. Or I'll have a pen in my hand and I'm just click, click, clicking it, completely oblivious to the noise it's making. 

And it's not even just at work, either. It bleeds into my personal life. I play chess, and we have these regular meetings... and chess is supposed to be this quiet, highly intense, cerebral game, right? You're supposed to sit perfectly still and calculate. But I'll be sitting there at the board, and if I don't have a pen to click, I'll find a stray cable tie in my pocket—because I always have zip ties and velcro cable ties on me from working on server racks all day—and I'll just be turning it, twisting it over and over in my fingers, bending the little plastic tab back and forth. I don't even realize I'm doing it. I'm just trying to focus on the board, but my hands are going a million miles an hour until somebody across the table finally gives me *that look*. 

You know the look. That sort of annoyed, tight-lipped stare that says, "Please stop making that noise or shaking the table." And I always feel terrible when it happens. I'll force myself to put the cable tie down and put my hands flat on my knees, but I swear, as soon as I try to actually think about my next move or focus on the client's problem again, my foot just starts right back up. It's incredibly embarrassing, honestly, to be a grown man who can't sit through a meeting without squirming.
Looking back, were you also easily distracted, restless, or had trouble staying seated or waiting your turn as a child?

Well, yes, actually. It's funny you ask that, because... well, it's not really funny, I suppose, but my mother still jokes about it to this day. She loves to bring it up at family dinners, which is always a treat for me, let me tell you. She'll say, "Oh, you've always been like this," and then she'll quote my old report cards from grade school. 

I mean, I was a smart kid, I really was. I grasped the material quickly, and the teachers always wrote that I was bright, that I had a lot of potential. But then came the "needs improvement" section, and it was always the exact same story, year after year, teacher after teacher. They'd write that I simply could not stay in my seat. I was always wandering around the classroom, sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or going to look at the class pet, or just standing up at my desk for absolutely no reason at all. 

And the blurting out... oh, man. If the teacher asked a question, I knew the answer, and I just could not physically wait for her to call on me. I'd just shout it out. I didn't mean to be disrespectful, I really didn't, it was just that the answer was in my head and it had to come out immediately, before I lost it or before someone else got to it. I couldn't hold it in. 

And then there was the homework. That was the most frustrating part, even back then. I would actually sit down at the kitchen table, do the math worksheets, write the spelling sentences, put in the effort... and then the next day at school, when it was time to turn it in, it would just be gone. Vanished. I'd tear my backpack apart, dumping out crumpled papers and old permission slips, but the homework I had done the night before was just missing. I'd lose it between the kitchen table and my desk at school. My mother still laughs about how she'd find my completed math homework a week later stuffed inside a cereal box or under the couch cushions. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it's just... I guess it's just never really gone away, no matter how old I get.
